rationale: Data: 6766 works, one coded passage each (n_passages=1), years 1800-1925; cutoff 1876 gives 752 early vs 6014 late works. Rate = count__domains__DISTANCE_TRAVEL / n_passages. Estimand: per-genre mean of work rates late minus early, averaged equally over 8 genres. Effect +0.052 (passage-rate units); 95% CI [0.032, 0.069] from 1000 stratified bootstrap resamples within genre x period. All 8 genres show a positive difference (+0.04 to +0.06). Composition checks: the share of late works is nearly the same across date_confidence levels (88-89%) and origins (89%), and mean n_editions (1.11 vs 1.07) and author productivity (20.4 vs 21.0) are similar, so year assignment does not look tied to this metadata. Robustness: high-date-confidence works only give +0.047 [0.022, 0.075]; within-origin estimates are UK +0.035, US +0.044, unknown +0.059; OLS with genre, origin, date_confidence, log editions and log author productivity, with SEs clustered by author, gives +0.052 [0.034, 0.071]. Decade means rise fairly steadily, from about 0.04-0.06 before 1870 to about 0.10-0.12 after 1880, so the change does not depend on the exact cutoff. Caveats: there is only one passage per work, so rates are noisy 0/1 values. The early period is small, and a few genre cells have 37-57 early works, some with zero hits. The domain labels come from automated or annotator coding and may drift over time. The corpus is a sample of surviving or digitized works, which can carry selection bias. The cited passage IDs only show where the construct is coded; they do not establish the trend.
